title.en: Which subject do we like most?

text.en: Rohan and Anjali want to know which subject their classmates like the most. They could just guess, but a good maths detective collects real answers, puts them in order and then reads the answer from the data. In this chapter you will learn how to ask a good question, collect answers, show them in a table and a graph, and use them to decide things.

Information that we collect to answer a question is called data. Every single answer we get is called a response. Rohan and Anjali wanted to find the most liked subject in their class, so they planned to ask every child. Before we collect data we must first decide what we want to find out.
The question we ask decides the answers we get, so it must be framed carefully. If Rohan asks, Which subjects do you like, children may name two or three subjects, and then we cannot tell which one is the favourite. If Anjali asks, Which subject do you like the most, every child gives exactly one answer and the counting becomes easy. So a good question asks for one clear choice, uses simple words and means the same thing to everybody.
Anjali and Rohan wrote short letters for the subjects. M stands for Mathematics, L for Languages, T for The World Around Us, A for Arts and P.E. for Physical Education. They asked all 45 children in the class and noted every answer as it came, one after the other, in a long list of letters. A long list like this is hard to read. It tells us the answers but it does not tell us quickly which subject is the favourite.
To make sense of the list we count how many times each letter appears and write the numbers in a table. Going through the 45 answers we get Physical Education 11, Mathematics 10, Arts 9, Languages 8 and The World Around Us 7. Let us check the total. 11 plus 10 is 21, 21 plus 9 is 30, 30 plus 8 is 38 and 38 plus 7 is 45, so every child has been counted once. Now the table answers our question. The most common favourite subject is Physical Education and the least common is The World Around Us. A table is easier to understand than the long list because each subject has its own row and its own number.
While counting a long list we can use tally marks. We draw one small line for each answer. After four lines we cross them with a fifth line, so every bundle of five is easy to spot. Counting in fives is quick, so the total is easy to find at the end, and we do not lose track or count an answer twice.
A bar graph shows the same numbers as tall and short bars. The longer the bar, the greater the number. Look at the graph on the board. The bar for Physical Education is the tallest, and the bar for The World Around Us is the shortest. A graph needs a title that tells what it is about, and labels that tell what each bar means and what the numbers on the side stand for. On the side the numbers go up in equal steps, here in twos, so we must read a bar by finding the number level with its top.
A pictograph uses small pictures to show data, and each picture can stand for one thing. Anjali and Rohan watched which colour of ice gola the children ate at lunch, and put one small picture for each gola eaten. The colour with the most pictures is the most popular, and the colour with the fewest pictures is the least popular. If the boys and the girls are recorded separately, we can also find which colour the boys liked most and which colour the girls liked most.
Sometimes we sort children into groups. In the activity, children are asked if they play only chess, only cricket, both or neither. We draw a table with four rows and two columns, one column for girls and one for boys. Then we can say who plays chess more, who plays cricket more, and how many children play both games. Every child must fit in exactly one row, so the numbers in all rows add up to the number of children we asked.
At the Bal Mela, Anjali and Rohan recorded how many fruit chaats and sandwiches were sold on three days. From such a pictograph we can find the total of each item, the day on which most were sold, and which item sold more on a given day. Adding the two items for each day gives the total sales of that day, and the largest total tells us the best day.
Data is useful because it helps us decide. If the canteen knows that most children like one fruit chaat, it can make more of it. A good conclusion uses the numbers. We say Physical Education is liked by 11 children, which is more than any other subject, and not just it looks popular. Next time you wonder about your class, ask one clear question, collect the answers, make a table, draw a graph and say what the data tells you.

problem.en: In a class of 45 children, 10 like Maths, 9 like Arts, 8 like Languages and 7 like The World Around Us. How many like Physical Education?

text.en: The total is 45, so the four known groups together must be subtracted.

why.en: 10 plus 9 plus 8 plus 7 are added first.
So 34 children like the other four subjects.

text.en: 45 minus 34 is 11, so 11 children like Physical Education.

problem.en: Read the bar graph. How many more children like Physical Education than Languages?

text.en: The Physical Education bar goes up to 11 and the Languages bar goes up to 8.

why.en: Read the number level with the top of each bar.

text.en: To find how many more we subtract: 11 - 8 = 3.
So 3 more children like Physical Education than Languages.

prompt.en: Explain how to find the favourite subject of your class and how to show it.

requiredIdeas.en: Ask one clear question with one choice
Record every answer and count with tally marks
Put the counts in a table and check the total
Draw a bar graph or pictograph and read the tallest bar

commonMisconceptions.en: A question that lets children give many answers is fine
The tallest bar is the smallest number
We do not need to check the total

points.en: Data is information collected to answer a question, and each answer is a response.
A good question asks for one clear choice.
Tally marks in bundles of five make counting easy.
A table, a bar graph and a pictograph show data clearly, and the tallest bar or most pictures is the most common.
The total of all counts must match the number of children asked.
